text:
Programs for Students

High SchoolUndergraduateGraduate



We hosted 30 High School internships, and tours for 6 teachers and 454 High School students from St Joseph’s High School, J. Percy Page High School, Old Scona Academic High School, Grandview Heights School, Harry Ainlay School, Archbishop MacDonald High School, Ottewell Junior High School, and the WISEST program (since 2016), USchool program (since 2016), and TeamUP (2017).
The students learn about arc welding processes and robotics.
Interns benefit from contacts to industry to get internships in the industry.
Schools benefit from know-how and technologies that are available at CCWJ.
Free access to our high-speed videos for teaching.
Award-winning interdisciplinary projects attract young talent and expose them to welding: CCWJ outreach program has been successful in getting people, and has won a first prize in the AWS poster competition at Fabtech 2015.




A total of 232, 4-month research projects with 168 individual students since 2010.
33 summer students and 56 international visiting students since 2010.
In-depth exposure to welding with a wide range of projects from practical to theoretical through formal classroom teaching and hands-on experience in research.
Possibility to become co-authors in research publications and CWA Journal articles.
Exposure to international welding research and gaining a solid understanding of current welding technology.
Participation in exchange programs and international internships.
Guest lectures by high-profile international visitors.
Interact with industry and develop an understanding of industry needs - and get help finding industry internships / co-op placements / jobs.



Multiple streams of studies: MSc in Welding Engineering, MEng in Welding Engineering, PhD, Post-doctoral research.
Two tracks:

Leaders in the practical application of advanced welding processes, metallurgy, and automation.
Leaders in the creation of new technologies in advanced welding processes, metallurgy, and automation.


Gain in-depth understanding of welding processes, science, and needs of industry.
Exposure to international welding research.

Solid understanding of current welding technology.
Hands-on welding experience.
Knowledge: understanding of welding fundamentals.
Resourcefulness: close familiarity with welding industry and practical considerations.
Leadership: CWA student chapter executive, CWA Edmonton chapter.
Flexibility: Able to discriminate important from secondary, myths from truth.
Communication: Open and clear discussion of ideas with the whole spectrum of welding professionals.
Team players: collaboration with international researchers and teamwork in the group.
Exposure: attend trade shows (Fabtech, GPS, etc.) and conferences (e.g. CanWeld, IIW).






CCWJ has a strong focus on Equity, Diversity, and Inclusivity
The CCWJ is a culturally diverse institution, with up to 13 different nationalities and numerous languages present. We actively and successfully focus on providing an equitable, diverse, and inclusive environment, and support our students in thriving as a lab member, and finding a career in engineering, science, and the welding industry. This support takes place on several levels: on a secondary school level we maintain an outreach program to local high-schools on both the applied (St. Joseph’s High School) and the theoretical side (Old Scona), which exposes students to welding and engineering and encourages them to consider a career in this area. We also participate in the WISEST program and we have hosted four female interns and three female summer students. When the economic downturn in Alberta made it difficult to find employment in welding for one of the female welding apprentices who worked with our lab, we used our contacts to industry and research to ensure she finds welding-related employment that allows her to build her resume, expand her experiences, and join the welding community as a successful professional.
We recognize that we are still facing challenges to improve our numbers of female students and indigenous students, and we are making active efforts and seek ongoing feedback on the effectiveness of these efforts. Faculty, staff, and students regularly attend workshops to ensure that the lab environment is inclusive and welcoming to everybody, and regularly engage external resources to adjust our strategies.

title: Stud Welder TRW
text:
Arc welds metal “studs” onto the base plate material with controller burst current. We use this to study various stud welding techniques and material combinations and their effectiveness. Used across industries for affixing any kind of stand off, bolt, or other stud type piece onto a base matterial. Commonly used for threaded connections, PCB standoffs, and many automotive parts.

Project
Title: Closed-Loop Microcontroller Torch Control In Welding Automation.
An automated vertical standoff system for a stationary GMAW torch will be designed in this project. This project is intended to improve the weld quality by regulating the current in gas metal arc welding process (GMAW) for this purpose an electro-mechanical system consisting of a linear guide rail and an electric actuator carrying the welding torch should modify the contact tip to workpiece distance (CTWD). The prototype uses a microcontroller in conjunction with sensors to acquire, analyze and control the vertical position of the welding torch in response to geometric changes in the surface of the welding plate that are sensed through the fluctuations in the welding current.
In GMAW, voltage and wire-feed speed are controlled and kept constant. An important factor that translates into a quality weld is to keep the CTWD constant, however due to imperfections in the material’s surface the CTWD changes translating into a change in current due to a direct relationship, creating discrepancies and thus bad quality in the weld. For this purpose, the automated CTWD-Torch control is being developed using a feedback control loop to tackle this perturbances and maintain a set point according to the client’s needs.

Project
No consensus exists between standards and codes when deciding the Charpy V-notch (CVN) notch location of the lowest toughness in the heat-affected zone (HAZ) of plasma arc welds. Although, general agreement exists on the most susceptible microstructures, translating this knowledge into a predetermined location is by no means trivial. The span of each HAZ subregion depends on factors such as initial microstructure, base metal alloying elements, and thermal history. Today, no code or standard has included these factors into their recommendations for HAZ notch location.
The objectives of this of this work are to:

Provide the welding community with a practical methodology for determining the CVN notch location in the HAZ region of lowest toughness.
Make this methodology “field-ready” for testing and validation at an industrial level.
Consolidate the work into a practical format for use in codes and standards such as AWS D.1.1.

title: Syed Irtiaz Alam
text:
I am an international student from Bangladesh and I joined the University of Alberta to pursue BSc in Chemical Engineering. I became involved with the Canadian Centre for Welding and Joining as a recipient of the Dean’s Research Award in Winter 2017. I worked on “Sensitivity Analysis on Bead Geometry in Manual SMAW Welds”. I received another research scholarship “Undergraduate Research Initiative” and continued to work full time in summer 2017, commissioning a semi-automatic orbital welding bug “Firefly”. Following that, I stepped onto an automation project regarding stand-off design for a vertical GMAW torch to control arc length. I have received several research scholarships and awards from CWBA, AWS as well as the University of Alberta. I have received 3x Dean’s research award, CWBA Award for undergraduate research, AWS Prize in Welding Engineering, CWBA Award for graduate research. Following my graduation of chemical engineering, I worked at Group Six Technologies, a local laser cladding company. Currently, I am pursuing my MSc in Welding engineering. My research focus revolves around automation and process control. I have presented my research to AWS Professional Program (x2 Chicago 2017 and 2019).

Prior Degrees
BSc, Chemical engineering


Project
I am working on the process automation of laser cladding for repair application. Three-dimensional worn geometry of the industrial part is digitized with a 3D scanner. The points cloud obtained from the 3D scan is divided into nominal and damaged segments by comparing with the brand-new 3D model of the part. Thus, the worn out locations are identified. These identified locations are tunneled to a parametric programming environment to generate tool-path for the robot. Subsequently, appropriate cladding parameters are set to carry out repair based on the substrate properties and target mechanical properties. These cladding parameters are coupled with the generated tool path to carry out a successful repair.

title: Goetz Dapp
text:

Goetz has a lot of experience in multimedia applications and technology; has directed, created, and worked on numerous theatre performances and concerts; has worked as a consultant on several multimedia projects; has worked in film and television; and is pursuing on an interdisciplinary research project that brings together Welding and Theatre.
